passage: Siddiq, five, sat on the kitchen step while his grandfather Thabo said, "Mrs Dlamini's hen laid a big egg this morning." "Really?" Siddiq's eyes went wide. "No way!" On the walk over he stretched his arms out. "It will be huge, bigger than a football!" In the coop lay an egg, large for an egg but ordinary. "It's big for an egg," said Thabo. "A football was what you hoped for." "Oh," said Siddiq. Then he held it. "It's still warm."

qa.q: Whose hen laid the egg?
qa.a: Mrs Dlamini's.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling on the walk, and what does his "Oh" at the coop suggest?
qa.a: Excited expectation, shown by wide eyes and stretched arms. The "Oh" suggests a flicker of disappointment, though the warm egg still delighted him.

qa.q: How did Thabo separate hope from fact?
qa.a: He named what was real, that it was big for an egg, and what Siddiq had hoped for, without mocking him.

qa.q: What is it like for Thabo when Siddiq's hope meets the ordinary egg?
qa.a: He probably feels a little sorry to disappoint him but wants to be honest. Siddiq holding the warm egg would reassure him.

grounding: Shows a child voicing disbelief and a big expectation, with an adult gently separating hoped from known.

passage: At circle time Nirmala Miss told the class that a new library corner would arrive on Friday. Tenzin, six, opened his eyes wide. "Really? No way!" "Yes, really." "It will be as big as the whole school," he said, spreading his arms. Nirmala smiled. "We'll see on Friday. I know there will be shelves and cushions. I don't know the size yet." Tenzin nodded and whispered to his friend, "Shelves and cushions. Maybe big."

qa.q: On what day will the new library corner arrive?
qa.a: Friday.

qa.q: How was Tenzin feeling about the news?
qa.a: Excited and hopeful, shown by wide eyes and spread arms. His "No way" could also have been a way of checking the news was real.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do to separate hope from what is known?
qa.a: She told him what she knew, shelves and cushions, and admitted what she did not, the size, without squashing his excitement.

qa.q: How might Tenzin's friend take his "Maybe big"?
qa.a: Probably as shared excitement, since it is a hopeful guess rather than a claim. The friend may join in.

grounding: Shows a child voicing disbelief and expectation, with a teacher separating what is hoped from what is known.

passage: I'm Deepika, Gopika's sister. When Mummy told Gopika her wobbly tooth would fall out and a new one would grow, Gopika's eyes went huge. “Really? No way!” Then she said, “And when it falls, the tooth fairy will bring me a bicycle. It will be big!” Mummy smiled. “We hope for nice things. But I don't know about a bicycle. What we do know is a new tooth will grow.” Gopika wiggled her tooth. I couldn't tell if she was disappointed or still hoping.

qa.q: What did Gopika say the tooth fairy would bring?
qa.a: A bicycle.

qa.q: What might Gopika have been feeling when her eyes went huge?
qa.a: She was probably amazed and surprised, perhaps a little doubtful, that a tooth could fall out and grow again.

qa.q: How did Mummy separate hope from what is known?
qa.a: She said it's fine to hope for nice things, but she didn't know about a bicycle, while a new tooth growing was known.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Gopika after Mummy's answer?
qa.a: Deepika can't tell whether Gopika is disappointed or still hoping, noticing she keeps wiggling the tooth.

grounding: A sister observes a preschooler's disbelief and big expectation about a tooth, and their mother gently separates hope from fact.

passage:
March: The mango tree flowered. Farhan announced, “There will be a hundred mangoes! It will be big!” Rafiq, his father, said, “We'll see. I hope so too.”
April: Rafiq showed him tiny green mangoes where the flowers had been. “No way! Really?” Farhan's eyes went wide. “Flowers turn into mangoes?” “Really.”
June: They counted the ripe mangoes. Twelve. Farhan's face fell. “Not a hundred.” Rafiq hugged him. “You hoped for a hundred. We didn't know. Twelve sweet ones is what we got.”

qa.q: How many ripe mangoes did they count in June?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when his face fell in June?
qa.a: He was disappointed, because he had expected a hundred mangoes and treated his hope as if it were certain.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say that helped separate hope from what is known?
qa.a: He reminded Farhan that he had hoped for a hundred but they hadn't known, and that twelve sweet ones is what they got.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel watching Farhan's wide eyes in April?
qa.a: He probably feels warm and amused, enjoying Farhan's amazement that flowers turn into mangoes.

grounding: Over months, a child expresses disbelief and big expectations about the mango tree, and his father gently separates hope from what is known.

passage: The monsoon clouds had been black all morning, and the village fair was supposed to start at four. Sumit sat at the door in his new shirt. “It will stop. It will be the biggest fair ever!” Zeenat Phuppo looked at the sky. “We all hope it stops. But we don't know yet.” Thunder rolled. Sumit's eyes went wide. “No way. Really raining more?” Phuppo sat beside him. “If it rains, we'll go tomorrow. If it stops, we'll run.” At half past three, the rain stopped.

qa.q: What time was the fair supposed to start?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when thunder rolled and his eyes went wide?
qa.a: He felt disbelief and worry that the rain might spoil his hope of going to the fair.

qa.q: Which choice by Zeenat Phuppo worked, and why?
qa.a: She said everyone hoped it would stop but they didn't know, and gave a plan for both cases, which helped Sumit handle not knowing.

qa.q: What would change if Phuppo had promised the rain would stop?
qa.a: If it hadn't stopped, Sumit would have felt let down and confused about what was promised.

grounding: A child states a hopeful expectation about the fair despite the rain, and his aunt gently separates hope from what is known.

passage:
On the metro platform, Darshan Bhaiya said, "Next stop, this train goes under the river."

Lalit's eyes went huge. "Really? No way! Under the water?"

"Under the water."

Lalit pressed his face to the window the whole time. When they came up again, he said, "And my birthday cake will be as big as this train!"

Darshan Bhaiya laughed. "You're hoping it'll be huge. What we know is Mummy ordered a chocolate one for our table."

Lalit thought. "A big chocolate one?"

"We'll see on Sunday."

qa.q: What did Darshan Bhaiya say the train goes under?
qa.a: The river.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he said, "Really? No way!"?
qa.a: He was most likely amazed and full of disbelief that a train could go under the water; his huge eyes show it. The cake claim afterwards shows he was also hopeful and excited.

qa.q: How did Darshan Bhaiya separate hoping from knowing?
qa.a: He named what Lalit hoped, a huge cake, and then gently said what they actually knew: Mummy ordered a chocolate one for their table.

qa.q: What would change if Darshan Bhaiya had promised a cake as big as the train?
qa.a: Lalit might have been very disappointed on Sunday when the real cake was ordinary size.

grounding: It shows a young child's wide-eyed disbelief and his big expectation, with an older brother gently separating what is hoped from what is known.
